source.subject: mathematics
source.usage: Official CBSE publication, freely available on cbse.gov.in; question text reproduced for study with attribution and a link to the original. Figures are not reproduced.
source.notes: Paper prints: Series GE1FH, 'SET~1' (text layer; stored as SET-1), Q.P. Code 30/1/1, 27 printed pages, 38 questions, Maximum Marks 80, Time allowed 3 hours. Session is not printed on the paper. English text is on odd pages 3-27 (Hindi on even pages 2-26); page 1 is the cover. This archive also contains a separate 'For Visually Impaired candidates' alternative paper (30 B_Maths Std for Visually Impaired.pdf), which was not used and is not reflected in this pack. This is the first Q.P. code (30/1/1) in the archive, matched to the Mathematics Standard section of the marking scheme (not the 241 Mathematics Basic section, which is a different subject code in the same zip). Severe, systemic extraction loss: this PDF's text layer drops nearly all Greek letters (theta/alpha/beta), minus signs, square-root signs, degree signs, pi, and stacked fractions/powers, apparently because the embedded math font lacks a Unicode mapping for those glyphs; in a few places (e.g. Q4, Q19-20 marking-scheme answers) a lost degree/pi glyph appears to have been silently substituted with a stray digit ('30' -> '300'). No PDF/OCR tooling beyond pdftotext was available to recover these. Every affected question is flagged in its own extractionIssues and downgraded to MEDIUM/LOW confidence rather than guessed. The marking-scheme PDF's text layer is generally cleaner (many symbols survive) and was used only to source officialAnswer and to determine the printed section/mark structure; it was never used to alter or 'fix' question text.

questions.text: A person is standing at P outside a circular ground at a distance of 26 m from the centre of the ground. He found that his distances from the points A and B on the ground are 10 m (PA and PB are tangents to the circle). Find the radius of the circular ground.

officialAnswer.text: ∠OAP = 90°. In right ΔOAP, (26)² = OA² + (10)² ⇒ OA = √576 = 24. radius = 24 m.

questions.text: In the given figure, O is the centre of the circle and BCD is tangent to it at C. Prove that ∠BAC + ∠ACD = 90°.

officialAnswer.text: In ΔOAC, OA = OC ⇒ ∠OCA = ∠OAC. Now ∠OCD = 90° ⇒ ∠OCA + ∠ACD = 90° ⇒ ∠OAC + ∠ACD = 90°, or ∠BAC + ∠ACD = 90°.

questions.text: Prove that opposite sides of a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle subtend supplementary angles at the centre of the circle.

officialAnswer.text: Value points include a correct figure (not reproduced here). ∠OAP = ∠OAS, so ∠1 = ∠2; similarly ∠3 = ∠4, ∠5 = ∠6, ∠7 = ∠8. Also ∠1+∠2+...+∠8 = 360° ⇒ 2(∠1+∠4+∠5+∠8) = 360° ⇒ ∠AOB + ∠COD = 180°. Similarly ∠BOC + ∠AOD = 180°.

questions.text: Prove that : tan θ/(1 − cot θ) + cot θ/(1 − tan θ) = 1 + sec θ cosec θ

officialAnswer.text:
LHS = tan θ/(1−cot θ) + cot θ/(1−tan θ)
= (sin θ/cos θ)/(1−cos θ/sin θ) + (cos θ/sin θ)/(1−sin θ/cos θ)
= sin²θ/[cos θ(sin θ−cos θ)] − cos²θ/[sin θ (sin θ−cos θ)]
= 1/(sin θ−cos θ) [(sin³ θ − cos³ θ)/(sin θ cos θ)]
= (sin θ−cos θ)(sin²θ+ sin θ cos θ+cos²θ)/[(sin θ−cos θ) sin θ cos θ]
= (1+ sin θ cos θ)/(sin θ cos θ)
= 1+ sec θ cosec θ = RHS

questions.text: Prove that : (sin A + cos A)/(sin A − cos A) + (sin A − cos A)/(sin A + cos A) = 2/(2 sin²A − 1)

officialAnswer.text:
LHS = (sin A + cos A)/(sin A – cos A) + (sin A – cos A)/(sin A + cos A)
= [(sin A + cos A)² + (sin A − cos A)²]/[(sin A – cos A)(sin A + cos A)]
= (sin²A+cos²A + 2 sin A cos A + sin²A+cos²A− 2 sin A cos A)/(sin²A− cos²A)
= (1+ 1)/[sin²A− (1− sin²A)]
= 2/(2sin²A− 1) = RHS

questions.text: Find the ratio in which the y-axis divides the line segment joining the points (5, −6) and (−1, −4). Also find the point of intersection.

officialAnswer.text: Let the ratio be k:1 and the point on the y-axis be P(0, y). 0 = (−k+5)/(k+1) ⇒ k = 5, so ratio is 5:1. y = (−4(5)−6)/(5+1) = −26/6 = −13/3. Coordinates of point of intersection are P(0, −13/3).

questions.text: Prove that 1/√5 is an irrational number.

officialAnswer.text: Let 1/√5 be a rational number, so 1/√5 = p/q where q≠0 and p, q are co-prime. Then 5p² = q² ⇒ q² is divisible by 5 ⇒ q is divisible by 5 …(i). Let q = 5a; then 25a² = 5p² ⇒ p² = 5a² ⇒ p is divisible by 5 …(ii). (i) and (ii) contradict p, q being co-prime. ∴ 1/√5 is an irrational number.

questions.text: A room is in the form of a cylinder surmounted by a hemispherical dome. The base radius of the hemisphere is half of the height of the cylindrical part. If the room contains 1408/21 m³ of air, find the height of the cylindrical part. (Use π = 22/7).

officialAnswer.text:
Let r is the radius of hemisphere and cylinder and h is the height of cylinder
h = 2r
Volume of air in room = (2/3)πr³ + πr²h
1408/21 = (2/3)πr³ + πr²(2r)
1408/21 = 8/3 × 22/7 × r³
r³ = 8
∴ r = 2 m
and h = 4 m

questions.text: Two dice are thrown at the same time. Determine the probability that the difference of the numbers on the two dice is 2.

officialAnswer.text: Total outcomes = 36. Outcomes with difference 2: (1,3) (3,1) (4,2) (2,4) (5,3) (3,5) (4,6) (6,4) = 8. P(difference is 2) = 8/36 = 2/9.

questions.text: Vijay invested certain amounts of money in two schemes A and B, which offer interest at the rate of 8% per annum and 9% per annum, respectively. He received ₹1,860 as the total annual interest. However, had he interchanged the amounts of investments in the two schemes, he would have received ₹20 more as annual interest. How much money did he invest in each scheme ?
extractionIssues: Rupee symbol (₹) lost in extraction before '1,860' and '20'; numeric values are intact

officialAnswer.text: Let Vijay invest ₹x at 8% and ₹y at 9%. 8x/100 + 9y/100 = 1860 ⇒ 8x + 9y = 186000 …(i). 9x/100 + 8y/100 = 1880 ⇒ 9x + 8y = 188000 …(ii). Solving (i) and (ii): x = 12000, y = 10000. Money invested in scheme A is ₹12000 and in scheme B is ₹10000.

questions.text: The diagonal BD of a parallelogram ABCD intersects the line segment AE at the point F, where E is any point on the side BC. Prove that DF × EF = FB × FA.
extractionIssues: Multiplication signs (×) lost in extraction between 'DF EF' and 'FB FA'; meaning unambiguous ('DF × EF = FB × FA')

officialAnswer.text: Value points include a correct figure (not reproduced here). In ΔADF and ΔEBF, ∠DFA = ∠EFB, ∠ADF = ∠FBE ⇒ ΔADF ~ ΔEBF ⇒ DF/FB = FA/EF ⇒ DF × EF = FB × FA.

questions.text: In Δ ABC, if AD ⊥ BC and AD² = BD × DC, then prove that ∠BAC = 90°.

officialAnswer.text:
AD² = BD × DC
AD/DC = BD/AD
Also, ∠ADB = ∠ADC
∴ Δ DBA ~ Δ DAC
∠DBA = ∠DAC
∠BAD = ∠DCA
Adding both
∠DBA + ∠DCA = ∠DAC + ∠BAD
∴ ∠BAC = 90°

questions.text: The perimeter of a right triangle is 60 cm and its hypotenuse is 25 cm. Find the lengths of other two sides of the triangle.

officialAnswer.text: Let the other two sides be x cm and y cm. x + y + 25 = 60 ⇒ y = 35 − x. x² + y² = (25)² ⇒ x² + (35−x)² = 625 ⇒ x² − 35x + 300 = 0 ⇒ (x−20)(x−15) = 0 ⇒ x = 20, 15. Sides are 15 cm and 20 cm.

questions.text: A train travels a distance of 480 km at a uniform speed. If the speed had been 8 km/h less, then it would have taken 3 hours more to cover the same distance. Find the speed of the train.

officialAnswer.text: Let the speed of the train be x km/h; reduced speed = (x−8) km/h. 480/(x−8) − 480/x = 3 ⇒ x² − 8x − 1280 = 0 ⇒ (x−40)(x+32) = 0 ⇒ x = 40. Speed of train = 40 km/h.

A school is organizing a charity run to raise funds for a local hospital. The run is planned as a series of rounds around a track, with each round being 300 metres. To make the event more challenging and engaging, the organizers decide to increase the distance of each subsequent round by 50 metres. For example, the second round will be 350 metres, the third round will be 400 metres and so on. The total number of rounds planned is 10.
Based on the information given above, answer the following questions :
(i) Write the fourth, fifth and sixth term of the Arithmetic Progression so formed.
(ii) Determine the distance of the 8th round.
(iii) (a) Find the total distance run after completing all 10 rounds.
OR
(iii) (b) If a runner completes only the first 6 rounds, what is the total distance run by the runner ?

A brooch is a decorative piece often worn on clothing like jackets, blouses or dresses to add elegance. Made from precious metals and decorated with gemstones, brooches come in many shapes and designs.
One such brooch is made with silver wire in the form of a circle with diameter 35 mm. The wire is also used in making 5 diameters which divide the circle into 10 equal sectors as shown in the figure.
Based on the above given information, answer the following questions :
(i) Find the central angle of each sector.
(ii) Find the length of the arc ACB.
(iii) (a) Find the area of each sector of the brooch.
OR
(iii) (b) Find the total length of the silver wire used.

officialAnswer.text: (i) central angle = 360°/10 = 36°. (ii) length of arc ACB = (1/10) × 2 × (22/7) × (35/2) = 11 mm. (iii)(a) area of each sector = (1/10) × (22/7) × (35/2) × (35/2) = 385/4 mm² = 96.25 mm². OR (iii)(b) length of silver wire used = 2 × (22/7) × (35/2) + 5 × 35 = 285 mm. (Official answer's stacked fractions linearised from the marking-scheme layout.)

figures.alt: Circle divided into sectors by straight lines through the centre, with spiral decorations; points B, C, A marked on the arc at the top right

questions.text:
Amrita stood near the base of a lighthouse, gazing up at its towering height. She measured the angle of elevation to the top and found it to be 60°. Then, she climbed a nearby observation deck, 40 metres higher than her original position and noticed the angle of elevation to the top of lighthouse to be 45°.
Based on the above given information, answer the following questions :
(i) If CD is h metres, find the distance BD in terms of 'h'.
(ii) Find distance BC in terms of 'h'.
(iii) (a) Find the height CE of the lighthouse [Use √3 = 1·73]
OR
(iii) (b) Find distance AE, if AC = 100 m.
extractionIssues: Sub-questions (i) and (ii) are not captured in the text layer (only their printed mark value survives for each); see page 27. The Hindi page (26) preserves the Latin fragments 'CD', 'h', 'BD' for (i) and 'BC' for (ii), suggesting (i) asks to express BD in terms of h and (ii) asks to express BC in terms of h, using the two angles of elevation.
